lines.text: An island of copper and Aphrodite, ruled in turn by Greeks, crusaders, Venetians, Ottomans and Britain, and divided still. This is the story of Cyprus.
About nine thousand years ago, farmers built a village of round stone houses at Choirokoitia, one of the oldest in the Mediterranean.
By around 1200 BCE, Paphos was a sacred city, a centre of the cult of Aphrodite, said to have risen from the sea nearby.
From the town of Kition came Zeno, who taught in Athens under a painted porch, and founded the school of Stoicism.
Centuries of Roman and Byzantine rule followed. Then, in 1192, the crusading Lusignan family made Cyprus a kingdom of its own.
In 1489 the island passed to Venice, which fortified its towns against a rising Ottoman power.
In 1570 the Ottomans came. Famagusta held out for months, but fell in 1571, and with it the island.
After three centuries of Ottoman rule, Britain took over the running of Cyprus in 1878.
In 1913 a boy was born who would become Archbishop Makarios, and lead his people to independence.
In the 1950s the Greek Cypriot fighters of EOKA took up arms against British rule, seeking union with Greece.
In 1960 Cyprus became independent, with Makarios as its first president.
Nikos Christodoulides, born in 1973, would become president in 2023.
But in 1974 the island was split by a line held by United Nations peacekeepers, running right through Nicosia.
It followed a coup backed by Greece's rulers and a Turkish invasion that summer, which left the north and south apart.
In 2004 Cyprus was one of ten countries to join the European Union, though the island remained divided.
Then, in 2012 and 2013, a banking crisis struck, and savers lost money to rescue the banks.
Crossroads of empires for thousands of years, Cyprus still waits to be whole again.
